title: What GLP-1s Are Doing to Your Gut (And Why Fiber Helps)
summary: GLP-1 medications can affect digestion, appetite, constipation, and the gut microbiome. See why fiber matters and how to get more through food.
body_markdown:
This article is for informational purposes only and does not constitute medical advice. If you have questions about your medication or how diet interacts with your treatment, consult your healthcare provider.


## Key Takeaways


- GLP-1s mimic a hormone your gut naturally produces, slowing digestion and reducing appetite. Those changes can affect your gut microbiome.
- Most people on a GLP-1 end up eating significantly less fiber than they were before, which can affect digestion, the microbiome, and how comfortable you feel day to day.
- Prioritizing fiber is one of the simplest ways to support your digestion and your gut microbiome while you're on these medications.


---


If you're on a GLP-1 medication like Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, Zepbound, or any of the others, you've probably heard a lot about what these drugs do for appetite, blood sugar, and weight. From a scientific and societal perspective, those effects are astonishing, profound, and very exciting. What you may have heard less about is what's happening in your gut at the same time, and why fiber turns out to matter even more on one of these medications than it did before.


These medications belong to a class called GLP-1 receptor agonists, and the most common ones are also structural analogs of the natural GLP-1 hormone, meaning they're built to look and act like the version your body already makes. We'll keep things simple and call them GLP-1s for the rest of this blog post.


#### How GLP-1s affect digestion and appetite


Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) is a hormone your body has been making for as long as you've been alive. It's produced by specialized cells in your gut called L-cells, which sit along the lining of your small intestine and colon. When you eat, these L-cells release GLP-1, which signals your pancreas to release insulin, slows down digestion, and tells your brain that you're satisfied[(Spreckley and Murphy, 2015)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26258126/) .


GLP-1 medications work by activating the same receptors your natural GLP-1 binds to, just for much longer—the engineered version is designed to last in your body far longer than your natural GLP-1 does. The result is more food held in the stomach, slower transit through the rest of the GI tract, and a satiety signal that stays on longer[(Jalleh et al., 2024)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39568409/) .


In other words, GLP-1s don't introduce a foreign function to your body—they mimic and extend a signal your gut has been producing on its own all along.


#### What changes in your gut on a GLP-1


GLP-1s change your gut in two ways at once: how your body processes food, and the kind and amount of food your body is getting in the first place. Both of those affect your gut microbiome, and they compound each other.


#### Slower digestion can lead to constipation


On the processing side, the same slowing that makes you feel fuller longer also slows everything that comes after. Food reaches your colon more slowly, and once it gets there, transit slows too. Slower transit means more water gets reabsorbed from stool than usual, which is why constipation is one of the most common side effects of these medications—reported in roughly 10 to 25% of users.


#### Eating less food means eating less fiber


On the intake side, GLP-1s reduce appetite significantly. Most people eat less food overall, and often different food: smaller meals, less variety, and frequently less fiber than they were eating before. Your gut microbiome depends on what you feed it at least as much as how that food moves through you. When both change at once, the environment your microbiome lives in changes on multiple fronts.


#### Your gut microbiome may change


A 2025 systematic review found that GLP-1s do measurably affect gut microbiota composition and diversity, but the specific changes vary by medication and most of the studies so far are in animal models[(Gofran et al., 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12029897/) . Though the picture is still emerging, what's clear is that this is a meaningful shift worth paying attention to.


#### How fiber supports gut health on a GLP-1


The most immediate reason: certain dietary fibers help with constipation. Soluble fiber, in particular, helps soften stool and keep things moving through a digestive system that's running slower than usual. It's a standard part of clinical recommendations for managing this side effect[(Gorgojo-Martínez et al., 2022)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9821052/) .


The deeper reason has to do with your microbiome. When[fermentable dietary fiber](https://zbiotics.com/blogs/journal/prebiotics-probiotics-and-postbiotics) reaches your colon, the bacteria that live there turn it into compounds called short-chain fatty acids—primarily acetate, propionate, and butyrate. These short-chain fatty acids feed the cells lining your colon, support your gut barrier, and play a role in immune signaling and metabolic health throughout the body. They're some of the most important things the microbiome produces, and they only exist[because of fiber](https://zbiotics.com/blogs/journal/fiber-for-gut-health-balanced-microbiome) .


Fun fact: those same short-chain fatty acids stimulate your L-cells to release more GLP-1 naturally[(Tolhurst et al., 2012)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22190648/) . So fiber isn't just feeding your gut microbiome—it's also supporting the same signaling system your medication is working with.


The challenge is that GLP-1s dramatically reduce appetite, and most people on these medications end up eating significantly less food overall, fiber included. The result is that the microbiome has less to work with at exactly the moment when supporting it would matter most.


*A note on timing: nausea tends to peak during the first few weeks of treatment or after dose increases, and the same guidelines recommend going easier on high-fiber foods during those nausea-heavy windows because they can worsen the slow stomach emptying that's causing the nausea in the first place. As nausea fades and constipation becomes the more persistent challenge, increasing fiber gradually is the standard recommendation.*


## Practical ways to get more fiber


Eating more fiber when you're barely hungry is genuinely hard, so the strategy is less about adding a lot more food and more about making the food you do eat count.


-


**Prioritize nutrient-dense, fiber-rich foods in every meal.** When you're eating less, every bite has more nutritional work to do. Beans, lentils, oats, berries, chia seeds, and leafy greens deliver more fiber per bite than most foods while still being nutrient-dense.


-


**Swap refined grains for whole grains.** Choose whole grain bread instead of white bread, or brown rice instead of white rice. Each swap adds about 1-3 grams of fiber per serving, and those small changes can add up to around 10 extra grams of fiber over the course of a day.


-


**Keep the skin on.** Apples, pears, potatoes, and cucumbers carry most of their fiber in the skin. Leaving it on is basically free fiber.


-


**Drink water with your fiber.** Fiber needs water to do its job. Without it, more fiber can actually make constipation worse, which matters more when GLP-1s are already slowing your digestion down.


-


**Build up gradually.** If you're not used to eating a lot of fiber, ramping up too fast can cause bloating and gas. Slower increases give your gut microbiome time to adjust.


#### Supporting gut health while taking a GLP-1


Most of the conversation around GLP-1s focuses on what they do for appetite and weight. The quieter story is what they're doing to your gut, and what your gut needs from you in return.


[Fiber supports your microbiome](https://zbiotics.com/blogs/journal/fiber-for-gut-health-balanced-microbiome) through a period of significant change, and it plays a natural role in the same gut signaling your body has been doing all along. In a moment when your body is recalibrating in real ways, fiber is one of the simplest and most consistent ways to support it.
